Abraham is the narrative subject of the teaching's mashal — his trust in God despite distress is the emotional/practical model the teaching recommends. However, Abraham is never declared 'IS a bechina of' anything in this Torah; he is a human example cited for his response (trust despite suffering). He functions as a narrative/eitza actor (his trust → divine comfort), not as a bechina node. Excluded.

The holy sparks are not declared a bechina of anything in this Torah; they are the positive result of the temporary capture of holy speech. Line 10 also mentions finding holy sparks among a great person's klipot. The gathering of sparks is the eitza consequence of temporary capture, not a bechina-equivalent of speech or Sarah. Excluded.

Line 4: 'שֶׁהֵם בְּחִינוֹת מִצְרַיִם, שֶׁכֻּלָּם שְׁחוֹרִים וּשְׁפָלִים' — the klipot-people ARE a bechina of Egypt. This IS bechina language ('בְּחִינוֹת'). However, Egypt in this Torah functions as a generic characterization of the dark/low domain, not as a distinct conceptual node with independent spiritual content beyond 'the domain of the klipot.' The equation מצרים = klipot-domain is a single identification: Egypt IS the klipot domain. Adding Egypt as a separate node would be redundant — it is subsumed within 'שלש קליפות' in Package 2. If the dataset later develops a standalone 'מצרים' node with distinct spiritual content, this equivalence should be captured, but for this Torah's packages it does not constitute a separate node. Noted but not separately entered as an addition.

This is an illustrative analogy for the soul's state — not a bechina declaration. The text explicitly introduces it with 'וּכְדִמְיוֹן' (= and this is like), marking it as a mashal/simile rather than a bechina identity. Excluded.

Line 8: a true tzaddik has the power to extract captured speech. The tzaddik is the rescuing agent — an eitza actor. He is not declared a bechina of anything in this Torah. He is parallel to Abraham (the rescuer in the Genesis narrative), but this parallel is implicit in the mashal, not stated using bechina language. He is captured as an eitza node in eitza_proposed_edges above, not as a bechina node.

Line 11 quotes Isaiah 9:19 with 'בִּבְחִינַת: אִישׁ בְּשַׂר זְרוֹעוֹ יֹאכֵלוּ' — 'they shall eat the flesh of their own arm.' This uses 'בְּחִינַת' language, making it technically a bechina statement for the soul eating itself. However, this verse is used as a proof-text describing the soul devouring itself in the wilderness — it is a fifth formulation of the soul's suffering alongside the Psalm 107 types. Its specific content (the soul consuming itself when starving) overlaps substantially with Package 3's 'חולי הנפש' node and 'נפשם בהם תתעטף'. Rather than adding a third sub-node to the illness cluster, this verse is noted as additional support for the 'חולי הנפש' node. The verse from Isaiah describes the same condition as Psalm 107's hunger passages. If a reviewer prefers to enter this as a separate bechina node ('אישׁ בשר זרועו יאכלו'), it would attach to Package 3.

analysis_notes.note_on_psalm_107_structure: Reb Nosson's commentary (lines 16-21) reveals that the Rebbe himself linked this Torah to the Talmudic statement (Berakhot 54b) about the four who must give thanks, developed in Psalm 107. The four archetypes — desert travelers (תועים במדבר), prisoners (חבושים בבית האסורים), the sick (חולים), and seafarers (יורדי הים) — are the organizing framework of Package 3. The bechina relationships in Package 3 are stated primarily in the commentary section (lines 17-18) using 'זֶה בְּחִינַת' language. This is structurally the same kind of bechina-through-commentary that appears in other Torahs where the Rebbe or Reb Nosson provides a retroactive bechina identification.
